name: Safety speed limits in high-consequence tasks
description: In consequential domains AI diffusion lags innovation by decades because safety demands make deployment slow; they predict slow diffusion will remain the norm there.
quote: the evidence that we have analyzed in our previous work is consistent with the view that there are already extremely strong safety-related speed limits in highly consequential tasks.

name: Validation cannot anticipate deployment conditions
description: Complex, unintelligible models make it hard to foresee every deployment condition during testing (Epic sepsis tool), so consequential deployments must go slowly; interpretability and auditing are not yet good enough to close this.
quote: A major reason is safety—when models are more complex and less intelligible, it is hard to anticipate all possible deployment conditions in the testing and validation process. A good example is Epic’s sepsis prediction tool which, despite having seemingly high accuracy when internally validated, performed far worse in hospitals

name: Regulation in high-consequence domains
description: Safety limits are enforced by regulators such as the FDA and the EU AI Act; they note credible concerns that such regulation is onerous enough to produce runaway bureaucracy.
quote: These limits are often enforced through regulation, such as the FDA’s supervision of medical devices, as well as newer legislation such as the EU AI Act, which puts strict requirements on high-risk AI.10 In fact, there are (credible) concerns that existing regulation of high-risk AI is so onerous that it may lead to “runaway bureaucracy”.11

name: Low intensity of use
description: Headline adoption numbers overstate impact because most users use generative AI infrequently, translating to a tiny share of work hours and productivity.
quote: But, because most people used it infrequently, this only translated to 0.5%-3.5% of work hours (and a 0.125-0.875 percentage point increase in labor productivity).

name: Workflow and habit change takes time
description: Adoption is about use, not availability; even a free, instantly available product requires people to change workflows and habits and learn to avoid its risks.
quote: Even if a new AI-based product is instantly released online for anyone to use for free, it takes time to for people to change their workflows and habits to take advantage of the benefits of the new product and to learn to avoid the risks.

name: Speed of organizational and institutional adaptation
description: Diffusion is capped by how fast organizations and institutions, not just individuals, can adapt; for past general-purpose technologies this took decades.
quote: Thus, the speed of diffusion is inherently limited by the speed at which not only individuals, but also organizations and institutions, can adapt to technology. This is a trend that we have also seen for past general-purpose technologies: Diffusion occurs over decades, not years.

name: Organizational restructuring discovered by experimentation
description: Electrification only paid off once factories were redesigned around production lines, with new workplace organization, process control, hiring and training, developed through cross-industry experimentation.
quote: What eventually allowed gains to be realized was redesigning the entire layout of factories around the logic of production lines. In addition to changes to factory architecture, diffusion also required changes to workplace organization and process control, which could only be developed through experimentation across industries.

name: Costly real-world errors throttle the feedback loop
description: Where errors are costly and the world cannot be simulated (self-driving), safety limits how much each iteration of the data-improvement loop can be scaled, stretching development over decades rather than hours.
quote: But this process took over two decades instead of a few hours in the case of AlphaZero because safety considerations put a limit on the extent to which each iteration of this loop could be scaled up compared to the previous one.

name: Capability-reliability gap for agents
description: Agents that automate real-world tasks are held back because reliability lags capability, and even moderately consequential tasks are too costly for agents to learn from real-world experience.
quote: This “capability-reliability gap” shows up over and over. It has been a major barrier to building useful AI “agents” that can automate real-world tasks.

name: Tacit organizational knowledge
description: Much organizational knowledge is unwritten and cannot be learned passively, so developmental feedback loops must be repeated per sector or even per organization, blocking rapid parallel learning.
quote: In general, much knowledge is tacit in organizations and is not written down, much less in a form that can be learned passively. This means that these developmental feedback loops will have to happen in each sector and, for more complex tasks, may even need to occur separately in different organizations, limiting opportunities for rapid, parallel learning.

name: Privacy and data-sharing restrictions
description: Organizations and individuals resist sharing sensitive data with AI companies, and regulation (e.g., healthcare) limits third-party data sharing, further limiting parallel learning.
quote: Other reasons why parallel learning might be limited are privacy concerns: Organizations and individuals might be averse to sharing sensitive data with AI companies, and regulations might limit what kinds of data can be shared with third parties in contexts such as healthcare.

name: Application development effort does not vanish
description: The bitter lesson applies to methods, not products: real applications still require large amounts of hand-built business logic, frontends and other components.
quote: In the context of AI-based product development, the bitter lesson has never been even close to true.23 Consider recommender systems on social media: They are powered by (increasingly general) machine learning models, but this has not obviated the need for manual coding of the business logic, the frontend, and other components

name: Social costs of experimentation
description: Pushing scientific and social-scientific knowledge beyond what humans already know requires experiments on people and organizations, which society will not (and should not) allow to be scaled rapidly.
quote: It will likely require interactions with, or even experiments on, people or organizations, ranging from drug testing to economic policy. Here, there are hard limits to the speed of knowledge acquisition because of the social costs of experimentation. Societies probably will not (and should not) allow the rapid scaling of experiments for AI development.

name: Judgment tasks resist evaluation
description: The tasks whose automation would most transform a profession (e.g., legal filings) have no single correct answer, so they are hardest to evaluate and benchmark performance says little about real practice.
quote: But for tasks that involve creativity and judgment, like preparing legal filings, there is no single correct answer, and reasonable people can disagree about strategy. These latter tasks are precisely the ones that, if automated, would have the most profound impact on the profession.

name: Real-world utility must be proven with professionals
description: Only building the application and testing it with professionals in realistic settings reveals usefulness; such uplift studies show modest, augmentation-style benefits rather than substitution.
quote: The only sure way to measure real-world usefulness of a potential application is to actually build the application and to then test it with professionals in realistic scenarios (either substituting or augmenting their labor, depending on the intended use).

name: Automation devalues automated tasks; humans move on
description: Once a task is automated its cost and value collapse relative to human labor, so humans shift to unautomated tasks and the AGI goalpost keeps moving; impacts land on different timescales per sector.
quote: Once we automate something, its cost of production, and its value, tend to drop drastically over time compared to the cost of human labor. As automation increases, humans will adapt, and will focus on tasks that are not yet automated, perhaps tasks that do not exist today

name: Herding and ossification in methods research
description: AI research herds around fashionable ideas and under-explores others; in high-volume fields new ideas break through less easily, slowing turnover of central methods.
quote: Unfortunately, throughout its history, the AI field has shown a high degree of herding around popular ideas, and inadequate (in retrospect) levels of exploration of unfashionable ones. A notable example is the sidelining of research on neural networks for many decades.

name: Compute and cost limits on methods
description: Hardware inadequacy held back deep learning historically and computational and cost limits still constrain new paradigms like inference-time scaling.
quote: Historically, deep neural network technology was partly held back due to the inadequacy of hardware, particularly Graphics Processing Units. Computational and cost limits continue to be relevant to new paradigms, including inference-time scaling.

name: Decline of open knowledge sharing
description: A shift away from the industry's culture of open knowledge sharing is a newly emerging slowdown on methods progress.
quote: New slowdowns may emerge: Recent signs point to a shift away from the culture of open knowledge sharing in the industry.

name: Legibility and control risks check end-to-end autonomy
description: Removing human specification and oversight from task boundaries to let AI run end-to-end raises safety risk by reducing legibility and control, which acts as a natural brake on ceding control.
quote: Eliminating some of these efficiency bottlenecks and having AI systems autonomously accomplish larger tasks “end-to-end” will be an ever-present temptation, but this will increase safety risks since it will decrease legibility and control. These risks will act as a natural check against ceding too much control.

name: Task specification effort
description: Unambiguously specifying what is wanted is a large share of the work, so specification and oversight remain human labor at the boundaries between AI-performed tasks.
quote: As anyone who has tried to outsource software or product development knows, unambiguously specifying what is desired turns out to be a surprisingly big part of the overall effort. Thus, human labor—specification and oversight—will operate at the boundary between AI systems performing different tasks.

name: Hard-to-automate physical job components
description: Citing Karen Levy on truckers, jobs bundle many physical and social tasks (inspection, loading, paperwork, yard moves) that are much harder to automate than the headline task.
quote: Could some of these tasks be eliminated by intelligent systems? Surely some can and will—but these components of the job are much harder to automate, and will come much later, than highway driving.

name: Poorly controlled AI is bad business
description: Market forces limit uncontrolled deployment because error-prone AI does not make business sense, so the shift to human-control jobs is market-driven and regulation reinforces it.
quote: We further predict that this transformation will be primarily driven by market forces. Poorly controlled AI will be too error prone to make business sense. But regulation can and should bolster the ability and necessity of organizations to keep humans in control.

name: Staged adoption requires proving reliability first
description: Organizations grant access to consequential decisions only after a system proves reliable in less critical contexts, a structural feature of how technology gets adopted.
quote: Long before a system would be granted access to consequential decisions, it would need to demonstrate reliable performance in less critical contexts. Any system that interprets commands over-literally or lacks common sense would fail these earlier tests.

name: Existing institutional controls around consequential decisions
description: Financial controls, safety regulations and similar institutional checks surround high-stakes decisions and constrain how much autonomy AI is granted.
quote: Existing institutional controls around consequential decisions—from financial controls to safety regulations—create multiple layers of protection against catastrophic misalignment.

name: Regulation that freezes categories
description: Regulation insensitive to the need for experimentation reifies categories, prematurely freezing business models, organizational forms and product categories, and miscategorizing risk by domain rather than task.
quote: Regulation that is insensitive to these needs risks stymying beneficial AI adoption. Regulation tends to create or reify categories, and might thus prematurely freeze business models, forms of organization, product categories, and so forth.

name: Misplaced burdens on model developers
description: Regulation blind to the model-developer / downstream-developer / deployer split saddles general-purpose model makers with context-specific mitigation they cannot perform.
quote: Regulation that is insensitive to these distinctions risks burdening model developers with responsibilities for risk mitigation related to particular deployment contexts, which would be impossible for them to carry out due to the general-purpose nature of foundation models and the unknowability of all the possible deployment contexts.

name: Binary automated/not-automated rules disincentivize new control models
description: When regulation only recognizes fully automated vs. human-in-the-loop, intermediate oversight designs incur full compliance burdens, discouraging adoption of better AI control models.
quote: When regulation makes a binary distinction between decisions that are and are not fully automated, and does not recognize degrees of oversight, it disincentivizes the adoption of new models for AI control.

name: Legal and liability uncertainty
description: Unclear application of liability law to AI deters adoption; clear rules (as FAA drone rules in 2016) spur it.
quote: In areas in which there is legal or regulatory uncertainty, regulation can promote diffusion. The application of liability laws to AI is often unclear. For example, this was the case with small drones until the Federal Aviation Administration regulated the nascent industry in 2016

name: Publisher wariness and bargaining asymmetry
description: Media organizations' justified distrust of AI companies and inability to bargain collectively limits incorporation of journalistic content into AI products.
quote: As one example, the incorporation of journalistic and media content into chatbots and other AI interfaces is limited by media organizations’ justified wariness of AI companies.

name: Underinvestment in complements: literacy, training, data
description: Diffusion depends on complements of automation (AI literacy, workforce training, digitization and open data) that are public goods the private sector will underprovide.
quote: One example is promoting AI literacy as well as workforce training in both the public and the private sectors. Another example is digitization and open data, especially open government data, which can allow AI users to benefit from previously inaccessible datasets. The private sector will be likely to underinvest in these areas as they are public goods

name: Energy infrastructure and grid reliability
description: Energy infrastructure constrains both training and inference, so grid improvements are needed for innovation and diffusion.
quote: Improvements to energy infrastructure, such as the reliability of the grid, will promote both AI innovation and diffusion since it will help in both AI training and inference.

name: Public anxiety about AI
description: High public anxiety about AI in many countries is a headwind that stronger safety nets and redistribution would reduce.
quote: Strengthening social safety nets will help to decrease the currently high levels of public anxiety about AI in many countries.

name: Loss of trust from rushed public-sector deployment
description: Deploying inadequately tested AI in government (NYC chatbot, DOGE) costs trust and legitimacy, while moving too slowly outsources functions to less accountable private actors.
quote: Moving too quickly will lead to a loss of trust and legitimacy, as was the case of the New York City chatbot that was evidently inadequately tested and made headlines for telling businesses to break the law.

name: Government procedure fetish / runaway bureaucracy
description: The administrative state's overly cautious, procedure-heavy approach keeps government from providing AI services it could, citing Bagley's procedure fetish and runaway bureaucracy.
quote: But the administrative state’s approach to these risks is overly cautious and has been described by Nicholas Bagley as a “procedure fetish,” potentially leading to a “runaway bureaucracy.”

name: National diffusion capacity (Ding)
description: Adopting Jeffrey Ding, the capacity to diffuse innovations through the economy differs greatly between countries and determines economic outcomes; progress is not automatic.
quote: An important consequence of the normal technology view is that progress is not automatic—there are many roadblocks to AI diffusion. As Jeffrey Ding has shown, the capacity to diffuse innovations throughout the economy varies greatly between countries and has a major effect on their overall power and economic growth.

name: Human-in-the-loop review erodes automation benefits
description: Requiring human approval of every AI action mostly destroys the benefit of automation, so it degrades into rubber-stamping or is outcompeted by less safe solutions.
quote: In most scenarios, this approach greatly diminishes the benefits of automation, and therefore either devolves into the human acting as a rubber stamp or is outcompeted by a less safe solution.

name: External bottlenecks immune to self-improvement
description: Limits on AI's power sit outside the system (in deployment), so recursive self-improvement of technical design cannot overcome them; diffusion barriers are not solved by capability gains.
quote: we don’t think RSI will lead to superintelligence because the external bottlenecks to building and deploying powerful AI systems cannot be overcome by improving their technical design.

name: Non-technological barriers persist past capability thresholds
description: Capability thresholds are necessary but not sufficient for real-world impact; reaching them will stress-test the non-technological barriers to benefits and risks.
quote: We see these capability thresholds as necessary but not always sufficient conditions for impact, and as and when they are reached, they will much more acutely stress our theses about non-technological barriers to both benefits and risks.

name: Model-to-product gap
description: Development splits into models and products; capabilities do not automatically become applications.
quote: On the development side, we emphasize the gap between models and products, or capabilities and applications.

name: User learning curves
description: Individual adoption is gated by learning curves and other individual adaptation, which change slowly though predictably.
quote: On the diffusion side, we differentiate between user learning curves and other aspects of adaptation by individuals, and the structural, organizational, or legal changes that might be necessary, which often require collective action.

name: Collective action and sclerotic institutions
description: Structural, organizational and legal changes require solving coordination problems or reforming sclerotic institutions, which is far more uncertain than individual behavior change (Air Traffic Control example).
quote: While user behaviors at least tend to change slowly but predictably, solving coordination problems or reforming sclerotic institutions — which are also prerequisites for effective technology adoption — are much more uncertain. As an example, consider how Air Traffic Control is stuck with technology from the middle of the 20th century

name: AI targets non-bottleneck workflow steps
description: In an already highly technological, regulated world, the workflow parts AI improves were already optimized by earlier tech; the true bottlenecks are regulation and other external constraints.
quote: We repeatedly find that the parts of workflows that AI tackles are unlikely to be bottlenecks, because much of the available productivity gains have already been unlocked through earlier waves of technologies. Meanwhile the actual bottlenecks prove resistant due to regulation or other external constraints.

name: Competitive arms races dissipate gains
description: In legal services and science, competition is so intense that AI productivity gains fuel escalation rather than societal value.
quote: In many specific domains including legal services and scientific research, competitive dynamics are so strong that productivity gains from AI lead to escalation of arms races that don’t ultimately translate to societal value.

name: Deployment is not diffusion
description: Instant deployment to hundreds of millions says nothing about diffusion, which depends on how many people actually use capabilities, how long, and for what.
quote: It is not enough to know how many people have access to capabilities: What matters is how many people are actually using them, how long they are using them, and what they are using them for. When we drill down into those details, the picture looks very different.

name: Low intensity of use (thinking models)
description: Nearly a year after release, under 1% of ChatGPT users used thinking models on a given day, illustrating how slowly capabilities become actual use.
quote: For example, almost a year after the vaunted release of “thinking” models in ChatGPT, less than 1% of users used them on any given day!

name: Professional guardrails in medicine
description: Malpractice liability, professional codes and medical-device regulation overlap to prevent doctors from delegating decisions to chatbots, keeping medical use mundane.
quote: there are many overlapping guardrails preventing widespread irresponsible use in the medical profession, including malpractice liability, professional codes, and regulation of medical devices.

name: Workflow adaptation is the hard part
description: The 100M-users chart captures curious early adopters only; the hard part of diffusion, users adapting workflows to incorporate AI, cannot even begin in two months and growth bends sharply afterward.
quote: Two months is not enough time for the hard parts of diffusion to even get started, such as users adapting their workflows to productively incorporate AI. As such, this chart is irrelevant to any meaningful discussion of the speed of diffusion.

name: Human behavior slow, organizational change slower
description: Learning curves exist, human behavior takes long to change, and organizational change takes even longer, even though instant deployment removes the access bottleneck.
quote: All our earlier points stand — learning curves exist, human behavior takes a long time to change, and organizational change even longer. But not using AI is somewhat of an active choice

name: Most adoption decisions are 'no'
description: Because deployment is instant, people constantly face adoption decisions, but the vast majority of the time they decide not to adopt, for rational or irrational reasons.
quote: even if it is ultimately the case that the vast majority of the time, people are deciding not to, for various reasons that might be rational or irrational.

name: Early adoption and integration pains
description: Developers now send forward-deployed engineers to work with deployers (John Deere, farmers) because integrating capabilities into real operations is a distinct, painful stage.
quote: In fact, model developers are starting to go beyond developing more useful products (the second stage of our technology development & adoption framework) and working with deployers to ease early adoption pains (the third stage).

name: AI community weak at finding new paradigms
description: Recursive self-improvement is far off because many fundamental research challenges remain, and the AI community may be unusually bad at finding new paradigms.
quote: More recently we’ve been thinking about the fundamental research challenges that need to be solved, and there are a lot more than we’d realized. And it is worth keeping in mind that the AI community might be particularly bad at finding new paradigms for progress compared to other scientific communities.

name: Complementary innovations needed for diffusion
description: Even past any capability threshold, many complementary innovations are required for AI to diffuse across industries, and diffusion runs at human and societal timescales.
quote: Even if general-purpose AI systems reach some agreed-upon capability threshold, we will need many complementary innovations that allow AI to diffuse across industries to realize its productive impact. Diffusion occurs at human (and societal) timescales, not at the speed of tech development.

name: Developing useful products and applications
description: First of four named diffusion bottlenecks: technical advances must be turned into usable products before they have economic effect.
quote: There are many bottlenecks to the diffusion of AI: developing useful products and applications, training the workforce to utilize these products, implementing organizational changes to enable AI use, and establishing laws and norms that facilitate AI adoption by companies.

name: Workforce training
description: Second named diffusion bottleneck: workers must be trained to use AI products.
quote: There are many bottlenecks to the diffusion of AI: developing useful products and applications, training the workforce to utilize these products, implementing organizational changes to enable AI use, and establishing laws and norms that facilitate AI adoption by companies.

name: Organizational changes to enable AI use
description: Third named diffusion bottleneck: firms must reorganize to make use of AI.
quote: There are many bottlenecks to the diffusion of AI: developing useful products and applications, training the workforce to utilize these products, implementing organizational changes to enable AI use, and establishing laws and norms that facilitate AI adoption by companies.

name: Laws and norms facilitating adoption
description: Fourth named diffusion bottleneck: laws and norms must be established that allow companies to adopt AI.
quote: There are many bottlenecks to the diffusion of AI: developing useful products and applications, training the workforce to utilize these products, implementing organizational changes to enable AI use, and establishing laws and norms that facilitate AI adoption by companies.

name: Humans are a moving target
description: As automated tasks lose value, humans move to unautomated tasks, so 'outperform humans at most economically valuable work' never triggers sudden mass displacement.
quote: But humans are a moving target. As the process of diffusion unfolds and the cost of production (and hence the value) of tasks that have been automated decreases, humans will adapt and move to tasks that have not yet been automated.

name: National diffusion enablers: digitization, cloud, training
description: Citing Ding, what matters geopolitically is diffusion capacity; China trails the US in digitization, cloud adoption and workforce training, all required for productive diffusion, and these cannot be fixed overnight.
quote: China lags significantly behind the US in several key indicators that might enable diffusion: Digitization, cloud computing adoption, and workforce training. All of these are required to enable the productive diffusion of AI advances across industries.

name: Growth bottlenecked by the weakest sector
description: Accelerating growth requires eliminating bottlenecks; AI's uneven sectoral effects mean long-run growth is capped by the slowest sector.
quote: The problem is that accelerating growth requires eliminating bottlenecks to progress. That’s harder than most AI boosters assume. AI will likely have uneven effects across sectors, and long-term growth will be bottlenecked by the weakest sector.

name: Production of findings is not the science bottleneck
description: Cheap generation of scientific findings will not unlock progress because producing findings is not what limits science.
quote: For example, while it is tempting to believe that cheap scientific innovation will unlock progress, the production of new findings is actually not the bottleneck in science.

name: Cultural, economic and political preconditions
description: Technology alone does not create progress; complementary innovations plus cultural, economic and political conditions are required (steam power did not industrialize Rome).
quote: More broadly, progress depends not just on the technology but on having the right preconditions — complementary innovations as well as cultural, economic, and political factors. If all it took to create the industrial revolution was the invention of steam power, the Roman Empire would have done it.

name: Laws, institutions and politics choking growth
description: Existing laws, norms, institutions and politics already block straightforward growth (e.g., infrastructure); the structural change needed to capture cognitive automation's benefits is vastly larger.
quote: Our current laws, norms, institutions, and politics evolved in a time of much less technological potential. They are already choking opportunities for straightforward types of growth, such as building more public infrastructure. To reap the economic benefits that broad cognitive automation can potentially bring, the degree of structural change that needs to happen is unfathomably greater.

name: Business incentives against unsupervised deployment
description: Strong business incentives, reinforced by regulation, keep AI from being deployed without adequate oversight regardless of capability level.
quote: We argue in the paper that there will be strong business incentives against deploying AI without adequate oversight, and that these incentives can and should be buttressed by regulation when necessary.

name: Bottlenecks to AI methods progress
description: AI-automated AI research cannot be arbitrarily accelerated because of the social nature of data collection and real-world interaction, compute and cost limits, and herding around popular ideas.
quote: But there are many bottlenecks to progress in AI methods, such as the social nature of data collection and real-world interaction that might be required for achieving certain capabilities, computational and cost limits, or herding around popular or intuitive ideas while ignoring the ones that enable true breakthroughs.

name: Society will not permit AI-run human experiments
description: Whether AI can replace a medical researcher depends on society allowing AI to run large-scale experiments on people, which it will not; similar constraints exist in virtually every job.
quote: whether AI can (autonomously) outperform a medical researcher depends in part on whether we collectively choose to allow AI systems to perform large-scale medical experiments on people. We shouldn’t and we won’t, which means that irrespective of the systems' capabilities, they cannot perform the function of a medical researcher.

name: Real-world messiness cannot be simulated
description: Real-world automation capability can only be known after diffusion because no lab simulacrum captures the world's messy complexity.
quote: Worse, until and unless we diffuse AI everywhere, we won’t even know if the system is theoretically capable of automating work in the real world. We won’t be able to set up sufficiently convincing simulacra of the messy complexity of the world.

name: Real-world usefulness is domain-specific; agents fail at costly errors
description: General capabilities must be made useful one domain at a time; generalist agents only handle low-cost-of-error generative tasks, hence no useful travel-booking agent yet.
quote: While AI capabilities can be general, making AI useful in the real world will have to happen in a largely domain-specific way. (The generalist agent aspect of o3 is misleading — it can only handle generative tasks where errors have low cost, not when you need it to operate independently in the real world.

name: Stochastic models need careful evaluation and integration
description: Products built on inherently stochastic models are hard; businesses must run careful experiments before automating processes, and agents are not drop-in replacements that bypass workflow integration.
quote: Building products on top of inherently stochastic models is challenging, and businesses should adopt AI products cautiously, conducting careful experiments to determine the impact of using AI to automate key business processes.

name: Domain-specific adoption hurdles need product design
description: Product builders need deep domain knowledge to find adoption hurdles; e.g., Cursor's UI for verifying AI-generated code at multiple abstraction levels, with other industries facing different obstacles.
quote: Companies developing AI products need a deep understanding of the domain to identify hurdles to adoption and build what businesses adopting AI want. For example, one key innovation of AI-enabled code editors such as Cursor and Windsurf is the user interface which allows programmers to verify AI-generated text at different levels of abstraction.

name: Millions of small process and policy adaptations
description: Impact arrives through countless mundane business-process adaptations and policy tweaks rather than a single technological leap.
quote: AI's impact on the world will be realized not through a sprint toward a magic-bullet technology but through millions of boring little business process adaptations and policy tweaks.

name: Unauthorized practice of law (UPL) liability
description: UPL rules make it illegal for nonlawyers (potentially including AI tools) to apply legal knowledge to specific facts; the threat of fines and criminal liability makes providers limit tool functionality or withhold access from consumers.
quote: While AI’s legality remains in doubt, the threat of UPL liability can inhibit its adoption. Without reform, developers risk fines and criminal liability if their AI systems provide legal advice. Organizations may simply be unwilling to provide access to users

name: Legal uncertainty and patchwork of UPL rules
description: The status of AI under UPL is unclear and varies by state; this vagueness and variation, more than regulation per se, deters new entrants who could deliver better services.
quote: To be clear, the problem with existing UPL rules is not that they are regulations and therefore stifle innovation. It is that their uncertainty and variation discourage competition from new entrants, including the kind that produces better legal services.

name: Law firm ownership / entity regulations
description: Rules restricting who can own equity in or share fees with law firms block outside financing and scaled business models, deterring the operational experimentation needed to deliver AI-enabled legal services cheaply.
quote: Separately, entity regulations that restrict financing for AI legal startups can deter the kinds of operational experimentation helpful for delivering legal services at lower costs.

name: Adversarial dynamics / relative-value arms race
description: Because legal outcomes depend on relative rather than absolute quality, productivity gains on both sides simply raise the equilibrium amount of work needed to achieve the same outcome, so per-task cost falls but outcome cost does not.
quote: Because legal outcomes often depend on relative rather than absolute quality, when both parties become more productive, the competitive equilibrium simply shifts upward.

name: Billable hours incentive model
description: Paying and promoting lawyers based on inputs rewards more hours and more output regardless of outcomes, reinforcing the arms race and absorbing AI productivity gains.
quote: The billable hours model, in which lawyers are paid and promoted based on inputs, only reinforces these dynamics: More hours worked drafting motions and reviewing documents translates into greater revenue for legal firms without necessarily improving outcomes.

name: Discovery abuse and expanding discovery scope
description: Digitization showed that lower unit costs of document review get absorbed by over-requesting and over-sharing; judges applying proportionality rules may authorize broader discovery as unit costs fall, keeping total costs high.
quote: because federal rules require discovery requests to be “proportional” to a case’s needs, judges might respond to declining unit costs of discovery (the cost of producing each document) by authorizing more expansive discovery plans, leaving total costs high.

name: No natural limit on additional legal work
description: In transactional work one can always do more research or add more provisions, so there is no ceiling on the capacity of extra legal work to soak up efficiency gains.
quote: Since one can always do more legal research or add more contract provisions, there is no natural limit on the capacity for additional legal work to absorb efficiency gains.

name: Human judges' adjudication time
description: The speed at which human decision-makers can resolve cases and understand documents caps how much AI can accelerate legal processes without sacrificing the human involvement society wants.
quote: The speed of human decision-makers (whether judges, lawyers, or clients) places an upper limit on how much AI can accelerate legal processes without sacrificing human involvement.

name: Flood of litigation overwhelming courts
description: Cheaper filing means many more disputes reach court; overwhelmed judges either delay resolution or delegate to assistants and judgeless courtrooms, lowering adjudication quality.
quote: If judges do not delegate, adjudicating cases will take longer as both the number of cases and the work each requires expands. Yet as the common legal maxim says: “Justice delayed is justice denied.”

name: Courts restricting access or banning AI
description: Judges may respond to AI-driven caseloads by tightening doctrines to keep litigants out of court or by banning/sanctioning AI use, counteracting diffusion at the cost of access to justice.
quote: Or they could try to limit the use of AI in the courtroom, perhaps by requiring lawyers to disclose AI use or banning AI entirely and sanctioning any violators. Both responses would counteract a flood of litigation work but come at the steep cost of sacrificing access to justice

name: Time for humans to understand contracts
description: Even if AI drafts contracts instantly, the parties still need time to understand what the provisions mean for their interests, which becomes the binding constraint on transactional work.
quote: If advanced AI reduces the cost of drafting contracts (perhaps it can instantly draft 50 perfect provisions), a contracting party, even with the help of AI, will still need time to understand what those provisions do and how they impact the party’s future interests.

name: Legal, technical and moral objections to AI judges
description: Article III likely requires human judges, hallucination and private-influence problems remain, and moral objections persist; AI in judging must be adopted deliberately rather than forced by an arms race.
quote: We find the legal (Article III, which establishes the federal courts, likely requires human judges),87 technical (hallucination and private influence problems),8888 and moral objections persuasive.

name: Legal services as credence goods
description: Quality of legal work is hard to evaluate even in hindsight, so buyers rely on prestige proxies and normal market mechanisms fail to reward cheaper, better AI-enabled services.
quote: legal services are “credence goods,” which means their quality is difficult to evaluate even with hindsight.25 The final outcome in a case reflects the cumulative effect of many smaller decisions, so it can be very hard, even for other lawyers, to evaluate whether legal services were provided effectively.

name: Workflow adaptation and user training take time
description: Better models do not immediately yield reliable legal products because firms must redesign workflows and teach users, which is slow.
quote: In our analysis of the practice of law, diffusion will likely be slow. Better models have not yet translated into more reliable legal products because adapting workflows to leverage AI and teaching users takes time.

name: Benchmarks lack construct validity
description: Task-oriented benchmarks overweight what LLMs are good at and miss the contextual reasoning of real legal work, so they cannot reliably tell the profession when AI is fit for use.
quote: task-oriented benchmarks lack construct validity because they “overemphasize precisely the thing that language models are good at” while failing to test the contextual understanding and sustained reasoning that characterizes consequential legal work.

name: Deskilling and disrupted junior-lawyer pipeline
description: Automating entry-level tasks removes the experiences through which junior lawyers build expertise, a hidden cost that emerges only over time and that benchmarks miss.
quote: Benchmarks can also miss hidden costs that emerge only over time, such as deskilling of professionals.111 Relatedly, by targeting entry-level tasks, AI can disrupt the pipeline through which junior lawyers develop expertise.

name: Political obstacles to expanding the judiciary
description: The obvious remedy for court overload, adding judges, is politically fraught and underfunded, so the human-adjudication bottleneck persists.
quote: Menell and Vacca acknowledge that “[i]ncreasing the number of federal judgeships has been fraught with political complications.”

name: Incumbent resistance to regulatory reform
description: Lawyers and commerce groups lobby to limit regulatory sandboxes despite scant evidence of harm; Utah tightened eligibility and authorized entities shrank.
quote: Despite scant evidence of consumer harm—Utah’s Office of Legal Services Innovation received only twenty total complaints —lawyers and commerce groups petitioned the Arizona and Utah supreme courts to limit these sandboxes.

name: Model shortcomings prompting regulatory caution
description: Bar associations cite current models' unreliability as grounds to treat AI chatbots as bordering on unauthorized practice, so capability gaps feed regulatory restriction.
quote: The New York Bar Association, concerned that the shortcomings of current AI models would harm consumers, has warned that “AI-powered chat bots now hover on the line of unauthorized practice of law.”

name: Deciding and specifying what to build
description: Requirements specification requires reasoning about user needs, market signals, organizational priorities and regulation; it resists automation and, if compressed, causes pain downstream.
quote: requirements specification (the profession’s lingo for this layer) takes surprisingly long, and if it is compressed, it leads to much more pain down the line. This layer is hard to automate because it requires thinking about user needs, market signals, organizational priorities, and in some cases regulatory constraints.

name: Verification and accountability for delivery
description: Teams must test, understand and take responsibility for what they ship; this deliver layer is not compressed by AI and remains a human bottleneck.
quote: At the other end of the sandwich, human teams need to be accountable for what they deliver. It is possible that some day in the future teams will ship mission-critical code without fully testing and understanding it

name: Deep human understanding of codebase and business
description: Both deciding and delivering require deep understanding of the system, business and environment, which engineers must still spend time building.
quote: (3) the deep human understanding — of the codebase, the business, and the environment — required to carry out both of these.

name: AI unreliability
description: Today's AI is unreliable enough that shipping unreviewed code would be an existential threat, so humans cannot exit the verification loop.
quote: today’s AI is so unreliable that such haphazard practices would represent an existential threat to software teams and their customers.

name: Liability laws and sector-specific regulation
description: Existing liability and sector rules already act as speed barriers keeping humans accountable, and can be strengthened as a deliberate control on the pace of AI impact.
quote: These speed barriers are already largely in place due to liability laws and sector-specific regulation, but can be further strengthened.

name: Collective choice to keep humans accountable
description: Society can use shared norms, law and policy to keep humans in control regardless of capability, a more resilient speed control than slowing model development.
quote: A central insight of AI as Normal Technology is that we can collectively choose to keep humans accountable through shared norms, law, and policy. This is a much more resilient way to control the speed of AI impacts and improve safety

name: Cost of supervising agents
description: Agentic engineering requires constant human supervision, which is surprisingly time-consuming and mentally exhausting, limiting realized productivity gains.
quote: As agentic engineering has become the norm, engineers are discovering that supervising coding agents is surprisingly time consuming. For example, Simon Willison, a prominent developer and chronicler of the AI transition, has noted how he is mentally exhausted by 11am from supervising agents.

name: Tacit knowledge and organizational capital
description: Workers' tacit knowledge is what lets organizations use AI effectively, so AI adoption works through slower hiring rather than layoffs.
quote: Firing existing workers results in the loss of precisely the tacit knowledge and organizational capital that allows workers to operate AI effectively.

name: Prototype-to-product gap
description: Executives see quick AI prototypes but not the 90% of work needed to turn them into finished products, leading to overestimated readiness.
quote: CEOs are uniquely prone to delusions about AI’s usefulness because they can build quick prototypes but can’t see the 90% of work it takes to turn it into a finished product.

name: Lack of mature, vetted AI applications
description: Companies announcing AI-driven cuts usually have no production-ready AI app to fill the roles; the product layer lags the narrative.
quote: “When we ask if they have a mature, vetted AI app ready to fill in those jobs, nine out of 10 times, the answer is no—and they haven’t even started.”

name: Low survival and security of agent-generated code
description: Much agent code never reaches commits and unsupervised vibe-coded commits introduce far more vulnerabilities, so production software still needs qualified engineers.
quote: only 44% of agent-produced code survives into user commits, that vibe-coded commits introduce vulnerabilities at nine times the human-only rate

name: Skilled judgment required for democratization
description: Past 'democratization' waves failed because the barrier is not syntax but the judgment and accountability needed to make good decisions.
quote: The barrier isn’t actually learning the syntax. It’s having enough skilled judgment to make good decisions while maintaining accountability.

name: Essential complexity of specification (Brooks)
description: Specifying correct software behavior is inherently hard; AI only removes accidental complexity, so no order-of-magnitude productivity gain follows.
quote: But some of it is essential, because specifying the correct behavior of software is itself hard. He presents a forceful articulation of why the “decide” layer of the sandwich is thick and resists automation.

name: Decision value migrates upward
description: As decisions become delegable to AI they stop being a competitive advantage, so human decision-making moves to higher-level problems and the decide layer never thins.
quote: once a decision can be delegated to AI, it is no longer a source of competitive advantage, and the value of human decision-making migrates upward. Software increases in complexity over time, so there is no ceiling to this process.

name: Fixed pool of consumer attention
description: More consumer apps do not increase usage because attention is finite, capping AI's impact on consumer software even as output multiplies.
quote: The former competes for a relatively fixed pool of attention; more apps published doesn’t mean more hours of app usage.

name: Adaptation / structural transformation takes decades
description: The fourth diffusion stage, reorganizing work and industries around AI, is the slowest, takes decades, and has barely begun even in software.
quote: Adaptation: (or structural transformation) — the fourth and slowest phase. Much of my talk today is going to be about that. I claim that this stage takes decades. It has not really started yet, even in a field like software engineering

name: Drop-in replacement fails; organizational reorganization
description: Like electricity in factories, AI cannot simply substitute into existing structures; reaping benefits requires reorganizing layouts, training, hiring and labor law, which took 40 years.
quote: But this idea of a drop-in replacement did not work. We keep hearing that term in the context of AI agents today — that they will be drop-in replacements for human workers. That did not work in the case of electricity.

name: Slow individual adoption
description: People are slow to adopt new technology, part of the gap between what occupations could use AI for and what they actually use it for.
quote: Why is there a huge gap between what people in various occupations could be using AI for and what they’re actually using it for? One reason could be that people are slow to adopt technology, and that’s certainly part of our framework.

name: Reliability of agents
description: Reliability, distinct from accuracy, is the #1 deployment concern and has improved only 5-10 points while capability shot up.
quote: Given that the #1 concern people cite is reliability, we wanted to try to measure whether reliability, distinct from capability, is a barrier to the practical usefulness of AI agents.

name: Inconsistency / unpredictable failure
description: A 70% accuracy that means random failure on any task is useless for deployment, and benchmarks do not distinguish this from consistent success on a subset.
quote: Or does it mean that on any given task it might unpredictably fail with a 30% probability? That’s pretty useless from a deployment perspective. Perhaps shockingly, none of the agent benchmarks that we looked into make a distinction between these two.

name: Operational safety and legal liability of automation
description: Unrecoverable failures like deleting production data impose costs and legal liabilities that make companies pull back from hasty automation.
quote: Many companies that hastily rushed to automate business processes using agents are recognizing the limits and costs, and even legal liabilities — like when an agent deletes production data.

name: General-purpose / high-stakes / automated trilemma
description: For now an agent can be only two of general-purpose, high-stakes, and automated, so AI stays a collaboration technology rather than automating workers away.
quote: For the time being, you can have only two out of these three properties in agents: general-purpose (a language model based agent that can be instructed to do different tasks rather than purpose-built for a task like traditional software); deployed in high-stakes scenarios, and automated.

name: Automation and collaboration agents not designed differently
description: Industry treats headless mode as automation without designing scaffolds and post-training for reliability, hindering successful automation deployments.
quote: Right now the industry is not treating automation and collaboration agents differently. If you run an agent in headless mode, I guess that becomes an automation agent. That is not a good way to look at it

name: Decide layer not compressed
description: Understanding requirements, specification and planning is not being compressed by AI and may be expanding.
quote: The decide layer: understanding customer requirements, developing the specification, planning, etc. That is not getting compressed by AI.

name: Deliver layer: accountability, integration, maintenance
description: Understanding code deeply enough to be accountable, plus integration, maintenance and testing, is not compressed by AI.
quote: The deliver layer: Understanding your code deeply enough to be accountable for what you release; carrying out integration into customer systems, maintenance, testing, etc. This layer is not getting compressed either.

name: Clinical trials
description: Medical treatments require trials with thousands of people over 10-15 years; this external bottleneck cannot be solved computationally in the lab.
quote: But we know that the hard part of developing medical treatments is clinical trials that often require thousands of people and 10-15 years. That’s an example of the fact that the bottlenecks to superintelligence are external.

name: Integration into existing systems
description: AI models must be integrated into the many existing systems organizations run, a downstream task not solved by model releases.
quote: There are many barriers: reliability (already discussed); integrating AI models into various existing systems; tacit knowledge from domains like medicine or law or various other professions that need to be made available to the models

name: Tacit knowledge not available to models
description: Professional domains hold tacit knowledge that is not in training data and must be gradually made available to models through adoption.
quote: tacit knowledge from domains like medicine or law or various other professions that need to be made available to the models

name: Regulation prohibiting AI use
description: Regulation often outright prohibits current AI use in productive settings, frequently for good reasons, and must be modified to enable adoption.
quote: regulation that often straight up prohibits today’s AI systems from being used in productive ways — in many cases there are good reasons for that regulation, but it will need to be modified in order to be able to enable adoption.

name: Inherent limits on prediction (chaos)
description: Many tasks resemble long-range weather prediction, where mathematical limits exist and are already reached, capping what more intelligence can deliver.
quote: Our position is that a surprising number of tasks are similar to weather prediction, in that there are inherent limits and we are pretty much already at those limits.

name: Evaluation is not scalable
description: Every capability increase creates new demand for domain-specific evaluation, which resists automation and absorbs human effort.
quote: LLMs and agents are general purpose. So each time capability goes up, it creates demand for evaluation in a legal setting or a journalistic setting or whatever other setting, and that’s not work that is scalable.

name: Human understanding essential to science
description: Science is not mere problem solving; preserving human understanding is central to its purpose, so AI solutions require new roles to back out understanding rather than full automation.
quote: In our view, human understanding is not some friction to be automated away. It is rather essential. It is central to the very purposes behind why we do science.

name: Human learning curves
description: Taking advantage of AI requires continual learning of new workflows and topics; the learning curve is steep and time-consuming.
quote: I find that I’m spending something like 10 hours per week just learning and experimenting with new workflows, as well as learning new topics.

name: Dependence spiral and skill erosion
description: Using AI for tasks one has not mastered erodes skills and control, so responsible users limit offloading until they master the task.
quote: It’s very tempting to use AI for tasks that I am myself not yet an expert at, because learning new things is of course very hard. But that leads to my losing whatever little skills I have in that task over.

name: Policy and politics against irresponsible deployment
description: Preventing dystopian deployments such as AI owning and running companies requires hard policy work, a deliberate societal brake on how AI is deployed.
quote: I think it will take a lot of hard work to ensure that we don’t irresponsibly deploy AI systems in this kind of fashion. But I do think we can get there. ... We’re going to need policy and we’re going to need politics, and it’s going to be hard

name: Political backlash against AI
description: If professions cede work to AI without setting boundaries, public backlash against AI will intensify, threatening deployment.
quote: If we simply roll over and accept that a lot of our work will be done by AI in the future, instead of setting clear boundaries, I think it will lead to an even stronger political backlash against AI than what we are seeing today.

name: Commodity trap at the model layer
description: Undifferentiated models, similar costs, free pricing and low switching costs push inference prices to marginal cost, threatening recoupment of the $4-8T buildout and a crisis of confidence.
quote: If the labs fail to escape the commodity trap, the consequences are primarily financial: a potential crisis of confidence in one of the largest capital buildouts in economic history, with ripple effects through the broader technology sector and markets in general.

name: Enterprise data locked in incumbent systems
description: The data needed to embed AI deeply sits in Salesforce, Workday and SAP, inaccessible to labs, limiting how far AI products can inhabit enterprise workflows.
quote: One complication is that the data that could help build moats typically sits on companies’ servers in established systems like Salesforce, Workday, and SAP, largely inaccessible to AI labs.

name: Enterprise resistance to digital workers
description: Because embedded digital workers create extreme lock-in and target labor budgets, enterprises are likely to resist this top-of-stack vision most.
quote: When companies sell digital workers, the total addressable market is the economy’s entire labor spend, far larger than companies’ IT budgets. But precisely for these reasons, the vision is likely to encounter the most resistance from enterprises.

name: Enterprise reluctance to share IP for training
description: Data flywheels have not materialized because enterprises are unwilling to let their data, environments and traces train vendor models.
quote: So far, enterprises have been skittish about allowing their IP to be used this way by AI developers, but this may change in the future.

name: Outcome measurement problem
description: Pricing on outcomes requires infrastructure to measure customers' business processes; without it metrics are gamed, so value-based pricing stays out of reach.
quote: Outcome pricing requires solving a challenging measurement problem. The labs haven’t built the infrastructure to measure and understand customers’ business processes, and to track — let alone price — different outcomes.

name: Labs lack embedded customer teams
description: Outcomes vary by vertical and firm, and labs lack the downstream visibility SaaS vendors built over decades through embedded customer teams.
quote: Besides, outcomes vary between verticals and between firms, and AI labs lack the embedded customer teams that SaaS vendors spent decades building in order to gain this kind of downstream visibility.

name: Incumbent distribution and customer relationships
description: Standalone labs must compete against Microsoft and Google, who own distribution, procurement relationships and bundling, on an uneven playing field.
quote: for AI labs, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, to move up the stack, they must compete with larger incumbents who enjoy many advantages, notably existing distribution channels and deep enterprise customer relationships.

name: Token capacity constraint
description: Compute scarcity currently limits inference supply, though the authors expect infrastructure and algorithmic improvements to make it temporary.
quote: While there is arguably a token capacity constraint today, we expect this to be temporary.

name: Organizational constraint at the implementation layer
description: Adopting Garicano and Saa-Requejo, the binding constraint where models are put to work is organizational rather than technical.
quote: in the implementation layer, where models are put to work and where the binding constraint is organizational, not technical. We largely agree.

name: Skill erosion from behavioral lock-in
description: AI tools erode unaided skill while building vendor-specific skills, creating dependence with stakes for workforce resilience and safety.
quote: skill erosion could have profound implications for workforce resilience, safety, and the distribution of power between people and AI systems.

name: Credence-good quality of AI knowledge work
description: For judgment-heavy work, buyers cannot verify AI output quality even after the fact, so they rely on trust and reputation, muting price competition and slowing switching.
quote: the quality of AI’s contribution is hard for the buyer to verify even after the fact, because there are no objective standards. That makes such work a so-called credence good, similar to lawyers and consultants.

name: Lock-in raising enterprise costs and concentration
description: If labs succeed at lock-in, costs rise for every AI-dependent enterprise and a few players become entrenched, making gains concentrated rather than diffuse.
quote: It would raise costs for every enterprise that depends on AI and entrench a small number of players in a position of structural advantage that will be difficult to contest later.

name: Procurement portability demands and antitrust scrutiny
description: Sophisticated buyers require portability before signing and contractual lock-in is visible to regulators, limiting commercial moats.
quote: Sophisticated enterprise procurement teams will demand portability before signing, and contractual lock-in is highly legible to antitrust regulators.

name: Bespoke deployment and workflow redesign
description: Transforming workplaces requires forward-deployed engineers and consulting partnerships, labor-intensive work that sits outside the product stack.
quote: AI companies are also pursuing bespoke deployment and workflow redesign — through forward-deployed engineers and partnerships with consulting companies. This doesn’t fit cleanly into the stack.

name: Overproduction drowns novel work
description: Scientists' attention is finite, so as paper volume explodes, genuinely novel work is lost in the noise and cannot reach the canon; AI-accelerated production worsens this.
quote: The key is that any one scientist’s attention is finite, so they can only pay attention to a limited number of papers every year. So it is too risky for authors of papers to depart from the canon. Any such would-be breakthrough papers would be lost in the noise

name: Publish-or-perish production incentives
description: Institutions reward measurable production (papers, grants) rather than progress, making researchers risk-averse; AI makes it easier to chase these meaningless metrics.
quote: Most obviously, automating parts of the scientific process will make it even easier for scientists to chase meaningless productivity metrics. AI could make individual researchers more creative but decrease the creativity of the collective because of a homogenizing effect.

name: AI worsens attention inequality
description: AI search and summarization tools concentrate attention on already-famous papers, making it harder for new ideas to break through, as Google Scholar already does.
quote: AI could also exacerbate the inequality of attention and make it even harder for new ideas to break through. Existing search technology, such as Google Scholar, seems to be having exactly this effect.

name: Scientists lack software engineering skills
description: Most AI-for-science is software development, but scientists have not adopted six decades of industry practices like testing and version control, so AI adoption produces errors.
quote: Unfortunately, scientists are notoriously poor software engineers. Practices that are bog-standard in the industry, like automated testing, version control, and following programming design guidelines, are largely absent or haphazardly adopted in the research community.

name: Code and data not shared or reviewed
description: Peer review does not cover code, and most papers fail to share code and data, so errors in AI-based science cannot be caught.
quote: While peer review is a long and arduous step in publishing a scientific paper, it does not involve reviewing the code accompanying the paper, even though most of the "science" in computational research is being carried out in the code and data accompanying a paper

name: Subtle AI errors hard to detect
description: It takes far less competence to use AI tools than to spot their errors, so flawed AI-based research spreads and wastes researcher effort for years before being uncovered.
quote: Unfortunately, it takes much less competence to use AI tools than to understand them deeply and learn to identify errors. Like other software-based research, errors in AI-based science can take a long time to uncover.

name: Widespread flawed AI-based research
description: ML errors already affect hundreds of papers across dozens of fields, and methodological flaws mean that AI research often fails to yield deployable tools (e.g., COVID diagnosis).
quote: These errors are not just theoretical: they affect the potential real-world deployment of AI too. For example, Roberts et al. found that of 400+ papers using AI for COVID-19 diagnosis, none produced clinically useful tools due to methodological flaws.

name: No incentives to correct scientific errors
description: Unlike markets, where bugs surface via tests and customers, science has few incentives to fix flawed results, so errors persist for years.
quote: Companies have strong incentives to fix errors to maintain the quality of their applications, or else they will lose market share. As a result, there is a strong demand for software engineers with deep expertise in writing good software (and now, in using AI well). This is why software engineering practices in the industry are decades ahead of those in research. In contrast, there are few incentives to correct flawed scientific results

name: Prediction-explanation fallacy prolongs flawed theories
description: AI modeling improves predictive accuracy without improving understanding, like epicycles; better predictions from wrong theories can keep fields stuck in existing paradigms.
quote: In other words, if AI allows us to make better predictions from incorrect theories, it might slow down scientific progress if this results in researchers using flawed theories for longer. In the extreme case, fields would be stuck in an intellectual rut even as they excel at improving predictive accuracy within existing paradigms.

name: AI industry lacks incentive for understanding-oriented modeling
description: Overcoming the prediction-without-understanding limitation would need radical changes to modeling technology, and the AI industry has little incentive to build it.
quote: Could advances in AI help overcome this limitation? Maybe, but not without radical changes to modeling approaches and technology, and there is little incentive for the AI industry to innovate on this front.

name: AI short-circuits human understanding
description: Progress depends on human understanding built as a byproduct of solving problems; automating solutions erodes this byproduct and the ability to train scientists, build theories, and generate new problems.
quote: If we use AI to bypass human understanding, or worse, retain only illusions of understanding, we might lose the ability to train new scientists, develop new theories and paradigms, synthesize and correct results, apply knowledge beyond science, or even generate new and interesting problems.

name: Incentives prize solutions over understanding
description: Using AI to build tacit knowledge would require reorganizing science, because current career incentives and norms reward solving problems rather than understanding them.
quote: Of course, AI can also be used to build up tacit knowledge, such as by helping people understand mathematical proofs or other scientific knowledge. But this requires fundamental changes to how science is organized. Today’s career incentives and social norms prize solutions to scientific problems over human understanding.

name: Adoption outpaces slow institutional norms
description: Scientific institutions' quality-control norms move slowly, while AI adoption in science has been headlong; adoption and quality control are decoupled, unlike in markets.
quote: Over the last decade, scientists have been in a headlong rush to adopt AI. The speed has come at the expense of any ability to adapt slow-moving scientific institutional norms to maintain quality control and identify and preserve what is essentially human about science.

name: Market quality control slows consequential deployment
description: In markets, failed shoddy deployments force reputation-conscious companies to deploy AI slowly for consequential tasks, regardless of the pace of development.
quote: market mechanisms exert some degree of quality control, and many shoddy AI deployments have failed badly, forcing companies who care about their reputation to take it slow when deploying AI, especially for consequential tasks, regardless of how fast the pace of development is.

name: Collective action problems in science
description: Individual researchers rationally follow incentives, so fixing AI's impact on science requires coordinated changes by journals, hiring committees, funders, and policymakers.
quote: Yelling at them is not going to help that much, because what we have are collective action problems. The actors with real power to effect change are journals, universities hiring & promotion committees, funders, policymakers, etc.

name: Meta-science underfunded and progress ill-defined
description: There is no clear construct for scientific progress or consensus on the slowdown's causes, and meta-science receives a tiny fraction of science funding.
quote: Despite recent growth, meta-science funding is a fraction of a percent of science funding (and research on the slowdown is only a fraction of that pie).

name: Incentive reform blocked by inertia and Goodhart
description: Efforts to replace production metrics consistently fail due to inertia, gaming of any new metric, and the fact that true progress is only identifiable retrospectively.
quote: But efforts to change this have consistently failed. One reason is simple inertia. Then there’s the aforementioned Goodhart’s law — whatever new metric is instituted will quickly be gamed. A final difficulty is that true progress can only be identified retrospectively, on timescales that aren’t suitable for hiring and promotion decisions.

name: AI-for-science tools target wrong bottlenecks
description: AI companies build science tools for flashy headlines and policy favor rather than for the real bottlenecks like error detection and understanding; results often fail to reproduce.
quote: They want flashy “AI discovers X!” headlines so that they can sustain the narrative that AI will solve humanity’s problems, which buys them favorable policy treatment. We are not holding our breath for this to change.

name: No evaluation of understanding and collective impact
description: AI-for-science tools are evaluated only on time saved, not on effects on researcher understanding or on community-wide attention, and no methods exist for the latter.
quote: Currently, only the first question is considered part of what evaluation means. The latter two are out of scope, and there aren’t even established methods or metrics for such measurement. That means that AI-for-science evaluation is guaranteed to provide a highly incomplete and biased picture

name: Agents lack judgment for open-ended research
description: Frontier agents given real research questions lacked judgment, creativity, and the ability to backtrack or respond to feedback, an unresolved bottleneck on the path to automated AI research.
quote: In this vein, our paper identifies an unresolved bottleneck, namely, the poor performance of frontier agents on open-ended AI research (though it remains to be seen if it is on the critical path to RSI).

name: Progress limited to verifiable tasks
description: Agents make rapid progress only where success is automatically verifiable; open-ended research without clear signals resists hill-climbing, so narrow gains may not yield broad RSI.
quote: Our view is that while faster progress is certainly possible on narrow tasks (such as improving efficiency), we don’t think it will lead to broad RSI or explosive progress.

name: Compute limits
description: Even if agent limitations are overcome, available compute could cap the pace of AI progress.
quote: Bottlenecks could include compute limits, the necessity of collecting data from real-world experiments, and others that we haven’t recognized yet because they are not currently blocking progress.

name: Real-world experimental data collection
description: Progress requires data from real-world experiments that cannot be sped up by faster AI.
quote: Bottlenecks could include compute limits, the necessity of collecting data from real-world experiments, and others that we haven’t recognized yet because they are not currently blocking progress.

name: Unrecognized latent bottlenecks
description: Bottlenecks like RL environments or energy infrastructure only become visible once they bind, so further unknown constraints likely await.
quote: For example, the importance of high-quality RL environments was not clear before they turned out to be useful for inference scaling. Similarly, the importance of building energy infrastructure for data centers was not realized before companies started investing hundreds of billions on data centers for training and inference.

name: Amdahl's law on overall progress
description: If many hard bottlenecks remain, even a hundredfold speedup on the AI-amenable parts yields only a small overall speedup, since the slowest component governs.
quote: Amdahl’s law would kick in: even a hundredfold speedup in the parts amenable to AI would only lead to a small speedup in the overall pace of progress, since progress is bottlenecked by the pace of the slowest component.

name: Capability-reliability gap in agents
description: Agents improve quickly on average accuracy but much more slowly on reliability metrics, and many benchmark-passing solutions would be rejected by real maintainers.
quote: we showed that even though agents are improving drastically in terms of capability metrics (such as average accuracy), they have improved much more slowly on metrics that measure reliability. Similarly, many agent solutions to SWE-bench tasks that were judged correct because they pass tests, would nevertheless be rejected by project maintainers.

name: Real-world messiness and incidental failures
description: Agents get stuck on CAPTCHAs, policy refusals, and infrastructure issues in unsandboxed environments, requiring human help to complete real tasks.
quote: Agents working on real-world tasks could encounter policy refusals, require solving CAPTCHAs, or encounter other infrastructure issues where they get stuck. This could negatively affect their performance.

name: Cost of frontier capability elicitation
description: Long-running agent tasks are expensive (C compiler ~$20k, iOS app ~$1,000), limiting how often frontier capabilities can be exercised or measured.
quote: Eliciting frontier capabilities is costly. Running large-scale, long-running experiments is expensive, making it impractical to achieve the sample sizes that benchmarks rely on. Anthropic’s C compiler cost ~$20k; the task we describe running below (developing and publishing an iOS app for CRUX #1) cost ~$1,000.

name: Non-functional software requirements unmet
description: Agent-built software sacrifices hard-to-specify properties like quality, reliability, maintainability, and security, so impressive artifacts are not usable products.
quote: For example, writing software has many non-functional requirements such as quality, reliability, maintainability etc. that developers might sacrifice when shipping apps autonomously coded using AI agents. Many concerns about Cursor’s browser and Anthropic’s compiler were actually concerns about these hard-to-specify properties

name: Dependence on human-built testing infrastructure
description: Agent reimplementations like vinext succeeded largely because of existing human-built test suites and infrastructure, limiting generalizability to other software domains.
quote: follow-up analyses highlighted persistent security limitations and low generalizability to other domains of software given the importance of human-built testing and infrastructure of both Vite and Next.js.

name: Scaffold security risks block adoption
description: Agent scaffolds capable enough to test the frontier (OpenClaw) carry security risks that may prevent real-world use.
quote: We recognize that OpenClaw has security risks in real-world use. We still chose to use it since we wanted to evaluate the capability frontier, while recognizing that security might be a bottleneck for real-world adoption.

name: Policy-mandated human steps
description: Platform policies require human involvement (developer accounts, 2FA dialogs that block synthetic input, pressing publish), so full autonomy is prevented by design.
quote: the agent couldn’t resolve requirements from Apple like intentionally preventing synthetic interactions (such as those from the agent) on sensitive dialogs like approving two-factor authentication. It needed to prompt us to log in to the Apple developer account.

name: Slow external review processes
description: Real deployment depends on systems and reviewers the developer does not control; the App Store review took ten days while the app took 45 minutes to build.
quote: This process typically takes several days and involves interacting with systems and reviewers that the developer does not control.

name: Agent setup effort
