description: Configuring permissions, accounts, and logging for an autonomous agent took eight person-hours and $50, a modest but real one-time hurdle.
quote: We estimate it took us eight person-hours of time and about $50 in API cost to set up the agent scaffold; this included configuring the virtual machine to ensure the agent had full control to take any actions

name: Visual reasoning and GUI operation
description: Agents' weakness at visual reasoning and operating graphical interfaces is a potential bottleneck to completing real-world tasks.
quote: We also wanted to test whether agents struggle with visual reasoning and GUI operation tasks, which might be bottlenecks to solving the task.

name: Diffusion lags capabilities
description: AI diffusion across domains lags capability improvements, which gives institutions time to adapt and build resilience.
quote: The diffusion of AI across domains lags behind improvements in capabilities. This allows institutions to adapt as AI systems become more capable.

name: Formatting and hallucination in knowledge work
description: Even on tasks agents mostly complete, persistent formatting errors and hallucinations (fabricated phone number, broken screenshots) remain bottlenecks.
quote: Epoch researcher Anson Ho had Claude Code and ChatGPT Atlas attempt to autonomously complete three challenging work tasks at Epoch: replicating an interactive web interface for a 40 parameter economic model, writing an article in Epoch’s style on AI progress in 2025, and porting an article from Google Docs to Substack and Epoch’s website. The project highlighted the persistent bottlenecks of formatting and hallucinations in successful knowledge-work tasks.

name: Verification requires domain expertise
description: Checking whether an agent actually succeeded at an open-ended task takes deep domain expertise and time, and long logs cannot be fully reviewed.
quote: Evaluating whether an agent succeeded in an open-world evaluation can be challenging. Verification of the agent’s work might require deep domain expertise and time, especially if the task is open-ended.

name: Speed limits between capability and economic impact
description: Economic impact requires building products, changing organizational workflows, and navigating regulation, which is why rapid job displacement claims fail to materialize.
quote: there are many speed limits between a new AI capability and its economic impact, including the need to build products, change organizational workflows, and navigate regulation.

name: Downstream physical steps for bioattacks
description: AI may lower information barriers, but causing bio-harm still depends on procuring materials, specialized equipment, and tacit know-how.
quote: AI may lower some information barriers, but bioattacks depend on many downstream steps: procuring materials, accessing specialized equipment, and applying tacit know-how.

name: State capacity sclerosis
description: Decades of veto points and proceduralism have hobbled U.S. state capacity, so the polycentric governance that resilience requires is hard to deliver.
quote: This is a tough sell given that state capacity in the United States has been hobbled by decades of accumulating veto points and creeping proceduralism.  As a result, unilateral actions by the executive branch are often seen as the way out

name: Multi-actor coordination for resilience
description: Resilience requires legislation, funding, cross-agency collaboration, early-warning systems, and rapid dissemination, tasks the federal government is not competent at.
quote: For resilience to be effective, the government needs to legislate and allocate funding, collaborate across agencies, build early warning systems, and serve as a resource hub for downstream actors and rapidly disseminate information to help them shore up their defenses. The U.S. federal government isn’t exactly well known for being competent at this set of tasks.

name: Under-defended institutions lack capacity
description: Schools, hospitals, power grids, and small agencies lack the capacity to adopt AI-assisted defense, so defensive diffusion needs investment and planning.
quote: That means AI-assisted red-teaming not just for tech companies, but for schools, hospitals, power grids, small businesses, and government systems that currently lack the capacity for defense.

name: Training data limits and rising cost
description: Readily available data is exhausted; more data costs ever more, including compensation demanded by copyright holders and reputational and regulatory costs.
quote: There’s always more training data, but getting it will cost more and more. And now that copyright holders have wised up and want to be compensated, the cost might be especially steep. In addition to dollar costs, there could be reputational and regulatory costs because society might push back against data collection practices.

name: Cost, not capability, blocks applications
description: Many applications possible with current models are not built or adopted because of cost, especially agentic workflows that call LLMs hundreds of times.
quote: That’s because capability is no longer the barrier to adoption. In other words, there are many applications that are possible to build with current LLM capabilities but aren’t being built or adopted due to cost, among other reasons.

name: Scaling is a business decision
description: Like CPU clock speeds and airplane speeds, continued scaling depends on whether it makes business sense, not technical feasibility.
quote: With LLMs, we may have a couple of orders of magnitude of scaling left, or we may already be done. As with CPUs and airplanes, it is ultimately a business decision and fundamentally hard to predict in advance.

name: Proof-of-concept to product gap
description: Developers mistook ChatGPT's thousand uses for product-market fit, ignoring the huge gap between demos and reliable, carefully designed products.
quote: They completely misunderstood the market, underestimating the huge gap between proofs of concept and reliable products.

name: Cost of inference
description: Cost, not capability, blocks many applications; cost also determines accuracy since retries improve success, so cheaper models mean more attempts.
quote: There are many applications where capability is not the barrier, cost is. Even in a simple chat application, cost concerns dictate how much history a bot can keep track of

name: Reliability vs software expectations
description: Users expect AI products to behave deterministically like software; 90% success is capable but not reliable, and it is unclear whether deterministic systems can be built from stochastic parts.
quote: But when developers put AI in consumer products, people expect it to behave like software, which means that it needs to work deterministically. If your AI travel agent books vacations to the correct destination only 90% of the time, it won’t be successful.

name: Privacy concerns for assistants
description: Useful assistants need training on and inference-time access to sensitive personal data (emails, screenshots), triggering outcry and backtracking.
quote: For assistants to do useful things for us, they must have access to our personal data. For example, Microsoft announced a controversial feature that would involve taking screenshots of users’ PCs every few seconds, in order to give its CoPilot AI a memory of your activities. But there was an outcry and the company backtracked.

name: Safety and security hacks
description: Accidental failures, misuse, and especially prompt-injection hacks that could leak data or spread AI worms must be addressed before assistants are trustworthy.
quote: At least theoretically, catastrophic hacks are possible, such as AI worms that spread from user to user, tricking those users’ AI assistants into doing harmful things including creating more copies of the worm.

name: User interface for supervision
description: Unreliable LLMs need interfaces that let users intervene without constant interruption; voice and ambient interfaces leave little room for error.
quote: But in applications where errors can be costly, such as flight booking, ensuring adequate supervision is more tricky, and the system must avoid annoying the user with too many interruptions.

name: Sociotechnical challenges and organizational integration
description: Even with solved technical challenges, organizations must integrate AI into products and workflows and train people, which takes a decade or more.
quote: These are sociotechnical and not purely technical, so progress will be slow. And even if those challenges are solved, organizations need to integrate AI into existing products and workflows and train people to use it productively while avoiding its pitfalls. We should expect this to happen on a timescale of a decade or more

name: Poor public perception from early misuse
description: DIY model access meant bad actors were disproportionate early adopters, and rushed integrations produced backlash, hurting public perception of the technology.
quote: OpenAI and Anthropic’s DIY approach meant that early adopters of LLMs disproportionately tended to be bad actors, since they are more invested in figuring out how to adapt new technologies for their purposes, whereas everyday users want easy-to-use products. This has contributed to a poor public perception of the technology.

name: Product development lags capability
description: Application development lags far behind capability, so existing capabilities are greatly underutilized; realizing them may take a decade or more, as with the web.
quote: The development of AI-based applications lags far behind the increase of AI capabilities, so even existing AI capabilities remain greatly underutilized.

name: Capability-reliability gap
description: A capability may exist without being reliable enough to remove the human from the loop, and reliability methods are application-specific and distinct from capability methods.
quote: even when a certain capability exists, it may not work reliably enough that you can take the human out of the loop and actually automate the task (imagine a food delivery app that only works 80% of the time). And the methods for improving reliability are often application-dependent and distinct from methods for improving capability.

name: Missing interface paradigms
description: Current AI products are like PCs before the GUI; new higher-bandwidth interfaces must be invented before capabilities can be fully used.
quote: Or consider this thought-provoking essay that argues that we need to build GUIs for large language models, which will allow interacting with them with far higher bandwidth than through text. From this perspective, the current state of AI-based products is analogous to PCs before the GUI.

name: AI companies neglect product engineering
description: Companies assumed generality exempted them from software engineering, and are now rediscovering that UX and product development are hard and need different skills.
quote: AI companies as well as their users are re-discovering that software development, especially the user experience side of it, is hard, and requires a broader set of skills than AI model development.

name: Adoption lags product development
description: Even once products exist, adoption lags for behavioral, organizational, and societal reasons that matter more for impact than capabilities.
quote: Finally, while product development lags behind capability, the adoption of AI-based products further lags far behind product development, for various behavioral, organizational, and societal reasons.

name: Societal tolerance for public experimentation
description: Business and social factors like whether society tolerates public roads being used for testing shape deployment more than technical feasibility.
quote: In the case of self-driving cars, one such factor is the extent to which societies tolerate public roads being used for experimentation. In the case of large AI models, we’ve argued before that the most important factor is whether scaling will make business sense, not whether it is technically feasible.

name: Exhaustion of readily available data
description: Scaling as usual ended with GPT-4-class models because they consumed most available data; new sources like YouTube video are locked behind one company.
quote: “Scaling as usual” ended with GPT-4 class models, because these models are trained on most of the readily available data sources. We already knew that new ideas would be needed to keep model scaling going.

name: Compounding unreliability in agents
description: An agent making dozens of LLM calls with even 2% independent error each becomes useless overall, explaining agent product failures.
quote: think of a flight-booking agent that needs to make dozens of calls to LLMs. If each of those went wrong independently with a probability of, say, just 2%, the overall system would be so unreliable as to be completely useless

name: Agent products too slow and unreliable
description: Flagship agent products (Rabbit R1, Humane pin, Devin) failed in practice because they were too slow and unreliable.
quote: The two main product launches based on AI agents have been the Rabbit R1 and Humane AI pin. These devices promised to eliminate or reduce phone dependence, but turned out to be too slow and unreliable.

name: Benchmark-driven overoptimism
description: Non-rigorous agent evaluation encourages agents that score well on benchmarks without being useful, feeding hype and product flops.
quote: This state of affairs encourages the development of agents that do well on benchmarks without being useful in practice.

name: Inference cost of agents
description: Because simple retries beat complex architectures, agent usefulness depends on dollar cost, which evaluations must control for.
quote: We show that such simple tricks can outperform complex agent architectures on the HumanEval benchmark, while costing much less. We argue that all agent evaluation must control for cost.

name: Leakage and reproducibility failures
description: Leakage and other ML errors affect hundreds of papers across 30 fields, likely the majority in many, undermining the usefulness of ML-based science.
quote: About 650 papers across all fields are affected, which we hypothesize is a vast underestimate — when researchers look for leakage systematically, in many fields they find that the majority of sampled studies commit the error of leakage.

name: Code and data not published
description: Researchers fail to release code and data (93% of pledgers did not), precluding reproducibility.
quote: There is also the basic problem of researchers failing to publish their code and data, precluding reproducibility. For example, Gabelica et al. examined 333 open-access journals indexed on BioMed Central in January 2019 and found that out of the 1,800 papers that pledged to share data upon request, 93% did not do so.

name: Science does not self-correct
description: Publish-or-perish, positive-result bias, no incentives for debunking, and near-zero retractions mean flawed AI-based work goes uncorrected.
quote: The root causes include the publish-or-perish culture in science, the strong bias for publishing positive results (and the near-impossibility of publishing negative results), the lack of incentives for debunking faulty studies, and the lack of consequences for publishing shoddy work.

name: Hype erodes skeptical mindset
description: Overoptimism makes researchers tweak models when they hit limits and trust suspiciously good results, a feedback loop that makes good research unpublishable against flawed baselines.
quote: since flawed research goes uncorrected, it becomes literally impossible to publish good research since it will result in models that don’t beat the “state of the art”.

name: ML code complex and unreviewed
description: ML code is more complex and less standardized than statistics, and reviewers do not check code, so coding errors are rarely found.
quote: Also, ML code tends to vastly more complex and less standardized than traditional statistical modeling. Since it is not peer reviewers’ job to review code, coding errors are rarely discovered.

name: Epistemology change exceeds field capacity
description: Adopting AI requires changing a field's epistemology, with validity re-litigated per field and model type, which no field can do in a couple of years.
quote: Adopting AI requires changes to scientific epistemology.4 No scientific field has the capacity to accomplish this on a timescale of a couple of years. This is not what happens when a tool or method is adopted organically.

name: Illusion of understanding
description: ML's selling point of discovery without understanding, now extended by generative AI, breeds errors and the illusion of understanding rather than scientific progress.
quote: And now scientists are embracing large language models and generative AI, which open up many new pitfalls such as the illusion of understanding.

name: Misdirected AI-for-science funding
description: Scientists already over-adopt AI to chase funding, so adoption incentives worsen things; money should go to training, meta-science, and reproducibility instead.
quote: Given the level of hype, scientists don’t need additional incentives to adopt AI. That means AI-for-science funding programs are probably making things worse.

name: Inherent limits to predictability
description: Some phenomena are intrinsically unpredictable, and researchers who ignore this mistake poor results for their own error rather than a real limit.
quote: when in fact they should strongly consider the possibility that they have run up against inherent limits to predictability. Conversely, they tend to be credulous when their model performs well, when in fact they should be on high alert for leakage or other flaws.

name: Prompting effort and scaffold overfitting
description: Headline agent feats may rest on thousands of lines of prompt and task-specific scaffolds, so it is unclear whether they transfer to other complex software tasks.
quote: Without these critical details, it is hard to know if the secret sauce is a better model or just more effort put into prompting the model.

name: Undisclosed human intervention and retries
description: Vendor demos do not define human intervention or report restarts, escalations, or retry counts, hiding how autonomous the agents really were.
quote: Nor does it clearly say whether any agents escalated to a human, whether the final run required any manual restarts, approvals, or fixes, or how many retries it took until the agent was successful.

name: Memorized code vs novel software
description: Toy operating systems are common in training data, so success may reflect regurgitation and says little about agents' ability to build novel software.
quote: Even if there was no direct copying, writing an operating system might be relatively easy for agents because of patterns memorized in the training data, so this doesn’t tell us much about agents’ ability to create novel pieces of software.

name: Vendor claims lack independent evaluation
description: Without released prompts, code, or logs, capability claims cannot be verified, so independent evaluators are needed to provide credible evidence.
quote: Google has not released the lengthy prompt, the code the agents wrote, or the logs from the run, which makes it impossible to independently evaluate the claims.

name: Diffusion takes a long time
description: Capability breakthroughs do not produce rapid societal effects; commercialization and deployment take a long time, which gives society time to react.
quote: Since diffusion of new capabilities takes a long time, that gives us plenty of time to react — time that we often squander, and then panic!

name: Missing supporting infrastructure
description: Breakthrough technologies deploy especially slowly because the surrounding infrastructure does not exist, as with the 40-year shift from steam to electric power.
quote: In fact, breakthrough technologies may especially take a long time to be deployed, because the supporting infrastructure just isn’t there. There’s a famous case study of why it took 40 years for electric power to replace steam power in factories.

name: Lack of verifiers in open domains
description: AI cannot become superhuman at legal reasoning the way it did at chess because there is no fast, accurate feedback on which arguments are good.
quote: AI can’t get that good at legal reasoning unlike reasoning in chess, because there is no way for AI to write millions of legal arguments and get immediate and accurate feedback on which ones are good and which ones aren’t

name: Limits of real-world knowledge
description: AI reasoning in domains like medicine is capped by the medical knowledge that exists in the world, the same limit humans face.
quote: Maybe it’s partly due to the limits of real-world knowledge. That is, AI can’t quickly become superhuman at medical reasoning because it is limited by the available medical knowledge in the world.

name: Brittleness outside closed domains
description: Reasoning systems that excel in narrow demos go off the rails in open-ended real-world settings; replacing human expertise in law or science remains unsolved.
quote: Over the decades there have been many other failures of reasoning systems, like IBM’s Watson, that excelled in narrow demonstrations but failed when you tried to use them in real-world settings that could depart from what they are trained for.

name: Policy backlash against deployment
description: Self-driving cars took 15+ years from public testing to deployment, and now face bans because policymakers failed to prepare.
quote: Instead, people are only now waking up to the reality now that these cars and trucks are already on the road, and are pushing policies like banning them.
